¶
'''backwoods''' (bak′wu̇dz′), ''n. pl.'' Wooded or partially uncleared and unsettled districts in the remote parts of a new country; hence, in the United States and Canada, any rough or thinly settled region far from the centers of population.
{{smaller block|The very ease with which books containing the world’s best literature were obtainable in the ''backwoods'' made our early writers copyists. {{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|He [Count Tolstoi] put into my hands a letter from some man living in a village in the ''backwoods'' of Pennsylvania.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXIV. 261.}}}}

'''backwoodsman''' (bak′wu̇dz′man), ''n.''; pl. ''backwoodsmen'' (-men). An inhabitant of the backwoods.
{{smaller block|<poem>The General Boone, ''backwoodsman'' of Kentucky,
Was happiest among mortals anywhere.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, viii. 61.}}}}

'''backworm''' (bak′wėrm), ''n.'' A small worm generally found in the thin skin about the reins of hawks. See ''filander''<sup>1</sup>.

'''backwort''' (bak′wėrt), ''n.'' The comfrey, ''Symphytum officinale.''

'''back-wounding''' (bak′wön″ding), ''a.'' Wounding at the back or behind one’s back; backbiting; injuring surreptitiously: as, “''backwounding'' calumny,” ''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2.

{{RunningHeader|backstay|415|Baconian}}on each side of the ship to the chain-plates, serving to support the masts.—'''Backstay-stools''', {{smaller|planking or pieces of iron projecting from the side of a ship, to which the backstays are made fast. They serve the same purpose for the backstays that the channels do for the shrouds.}}—'''Traveling backstays''', {{smaller|backstays fitted with a traveler which slides up and down with the topsail-yard. The principal support for the mast is thus kept at that part which is just above the yard. [Not now in use.]}} '''back-step''' (bak′step), ''n.'' A rearward movement of a squad or body of troops, without change of front. '''backster1†''', ''n.'' See ''baxter''. '''backster2''' (bak′stėr), ''n.''   [Etym. uncertain.]   A flat piece of wood or cork fastened on the feet for walking over loose beach.   ''N. E. D.'' '''backstitch''' (bak′stich), ''n.'' A method of sewing in which each stitch overlaps or doubles back on the preceding one, the needle entering behind the thread at the end of the stitch already made and coming out in front of it. '''backstitch''' (bak′stich), ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' To sew with stitches which overlap each other. See ''backstitch, n.'' '''backstone''' (bak′stōn), ''n.''   [E. dial., = ''bakestone'', < ''bake'' + ''stone''.]   The heated stone on which oat-cake is baked. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] '''back-stop''' (bak′stop), ''n.'' In ''base-ball'', a fence placed a short distance behind the catcher to stop the ball if he fails to catch it. '''back-strap''' (bak′strap), ''n.'' A broad strap passing along the middle of a horse’s back from the upper hame-strap to the crupper or a point of junction with the hip-straps in a wagon-harness, and in a carriage-harness from the gigsaddle to the crupper.   ''E. H. Knight.'' '''back-strapped''' (bak′strapt), ''p. a.'' Carried by head-winds to the back of a cape or promontory: said of a ship. '''back-stream''' (bak′strēm), ''n.'' A current running against the regular course of the stream; an up-stream. '''back-string''' (bak′string), ''n.'' A leading-string by which a child is supported or guided from behind. {{smaller block|The ''back-string'' and the bib. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 228.}}}} '''back-stroke''' (bak′strōk), ''n.'' '''1.''' A blow or stroke in return.—'''2.''' A backhanded stroke; a back-hander. {{smaller block|My uncle Toby never took this ''back-stroke'' of my father’s at his hobby-horse kindly. {{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, vi. 31.}}}} '''back-swimmer''' (bak′swim″ėr), ''n.'' Same as ''boat-fly''. '''back-sword''' (bak′sōrd), ''n.'' '''1.''' A sword with one sharp edge, used for cutting rather than thrusting, sometimes curved, and frequently straight. {{smaller|It usually had a basket-hilt, and was the common weapon of citizens and country people when the rapier and afterward the small-sword were worn by gentlemen.}} '''2.''' A cudgel fitted with a basket-hilt, used for a particular kind of single-stick play.—'''3.''' A cudgel-play in which the back-sword (in sense 2) is used, peculiar to certain counties of England, and still kept up at festivals and the like in the attempt to preserve old customs. {{smaller|The guard is with the left arm, and the object of each player is to break the skin of his adversary’s forehead so as to draw blood.}} '''back-tack''' (bak′tak), ''n.'' In ''Scots law'', a tack or lease connected with wadsets or mortgages, by which the possession of the land is returned to the proprietor on payment of a rent corresponding to the interest of the money advanced. See ''wadset.'' '''back-tool''' (bak′töl), ''n.'' Any tool, either fillet or roll, used by bookbinders in decorating the curved surface of the back of a book. '''back-trick†''' (bak′trik), ''n.'' A caper backward in dancing. {{smaller block|I have the ''back-trick'' simply as strong as any man in Illyria. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 3.}}}} '''backward, backwards''' (bak′wärd, -wärdz), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''bakward, bacward'', adv., by apheresis for ''abackward'', < ''abak'', adv., back, + ''-ward, -wards.'']   '''1.''' In the direction of the back: as, to throw the arms ''backward.''—'''2.''' With the back first in the direction of motion: as, to walk ''backward;'' to fall ''backward.'' {{smaller block|He [Eli] fell from off the seat ''backward'', . . . and his neck brake. {{right|1 Sam. iv. 18.}}}} {{smaller block|Thou wilt fall ''backward.'' {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 3.}}}} '''3.''' In the direction from which one has come; toward that which is or has been left behind: as, he glanced ''backward.''—'''4.''' Toward bygone times or events; toward that which is past in time: as, to look ''backward'' to the last century. {{smaller block|The lights of memory ''backward'' stream. {{right|''Whittier'', Memories.}}}} '''5.''' In or by reflection; reflexively. {{smaller block|The mind can ''backward'' cast Upon herself her understanding light. {{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Introd. to Immortal. of Soul.}}}} '''6.''' In time past; ago. {{smaller block|Some reigns ''backward.'' {{right|''Locke.''}}}} '''7.''' In an opposite or contrary direction. {{smaller block|For every two steps they made forwards and upwards they slipped one ''backwards.'' {{right|''Lady Brassey'', Voyage of Sunbeam, I. ii.}}}} '''8.''' In an opposite or reverse order; from the end toward the beginning; in an order contrary to the natural order: as, to read or spell ''backward;'' hence, perversely; in a wrong or perverse manner. {{smaller block|I never yet saw man, How wise, how noble, young, how rarely featur’d, But she would spell him ''backward.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The gospel of Christ is read ''backwards'', when that world which he came to save is regarded as a world which it is a merit to abandon. {{right|''C. E. Norton'', Travel and Study in Italy, p. 47.}}}} '''9.''' From a better to a worse state; retrogressively. {{smaller block|The work went ''backward'' ; and the more he strove T’ advance the suit, the farther from her love. ''Dryden.''}} {{smaller|'''Backward and forward''', to and fro.—'''To ring bells backward''', to give an alarm by ringing the bells of a chime in the wrong order, beginning with the bass bell.}} {{smaller block|The ''bells'' they ''ring backward'', the drums they are beat. {{right|''Scott'', Bonnie Dundee.}}}} '''backward''' (back′wärd), ''a.''   [< ''backward, adv.'']   '''1.''' Directed to the back or rear: as, “a ''backward'' look,” ''Shak.'', Sonnets, lix.—'''2.''' Reversed; returning; directed to or toward the original starting-point: as, a ''backward'' movement or journey. {{smaller block|And now they do re-stem Their ''backward'' course. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3.}}}} '''3.''' Done in reverse order; done in an order contrary to the natural order, as in repeating a sentence from the end to the beginning. {{smaller block|Without his rod reversed, And ''backward'' mutters of dissevering power, We cannot free the lady. {{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 817.}}}} '''4.''' Being in, or placed at, the back. {{smaller block|Four legs and two voices. . . . His forward voice now is to speak well of his friend; his ''backward'' voice is to utter foul speeches, and to detract. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2.}}}} '''5.''' Slow; sluggish; unprogressive; unadvanced; behind in progress: as, a ''backward'' learner. {{smaller block|Brigandage survives only in out-of-the-way corners of the most ''backward'' countries of Christendom, such as Spain and Sicily. {{right|''J. Fiske'', Evolutionist, p. 229.}}}} '''6.''' Late; behind in time; coming after something else, or after the usual time: as, ''backward'' fruits; the season is ''backward.'' {{smaller block|A dry, cold, ''backward'' spring, easterly winds. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, April 15, 1688.}}}} '''7.''' Holding back; averse; reluctant; hesitating. {{smaller block|The mind is ''backward'' to undergo the fatigue of weighing every argument. {{right|''Watts.''}}}} {{smaller block|For wiser brutes were ''backward'' to be slaves. {{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest, l. 50.}}}} '''8.''' Timid; bashful; retiring in disposition; modest.—'''9.''' Reaching back into the past; already past. {{smaller block|Flies unconscious o’er each ''backward'' year. {{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, ii. 24.}}}} '''backward†''' (bak′wärd), ''n.''   [< ''backward, a.'']   The things or state behind or past. {{smaller block|What see’st thou else In the dark ''backward'' and abysm of time? {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2.}}}} '''backward†''' (bak′wärd), ''v. t.''   [< ''backward, adv.'']   To obstruct; keep back; retard; delay. {{smaller block|Doth clog and ''backward'' us. {{right|''Hammond'', Sermons, xv.}}}} '''backwardation''' (bak-wär-dā′shọn), ''n.''   [< ''backward, v.'', + ''-ation.'']   On the London Stock Exchange, the premium paid by a seller of stock for the privilege of postponing its delivery to the buyer until the next fortnightly settling-day. See ''contango.'' '''backwardly''' (bak′wärd-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a backward direction. {{smaller block|The mandible is extremely massive and has a ''backwardly'' produced angle. {{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 320.}}}} '''2.''' Unwillingly; reluctantly; aversely; perversely; ill. {{smaller block|I was the first man That e’er receiv’d gift from him; And does he think so ''backwardly'' of me now, That I’ll requite it last? {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 3.}}}} '''backwardness''' (bak′wärd-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being backward. {{smaller|(''a'') Backward state as regards progress; slowness; tardiness: as, the ''backwardness'' of the spring. (''b'') Unwillingness; reluctance: dilatoriness or dullness in action.}} {{smaller block|Our ''backwardness'' to good works. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury.''}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') Bashfulness; shyness.}} '''backwards''', ''adv.'' See ''backward.'' '''back-washed''' (bak′wosht), ''a.'' Cleansed from oil, as wool after combing. '''back-water''' (bak′wâ″tėr), ''n.'' '''1†.''' Water flowing in from behind.—'''2.''' Water thrown back by the turning of a water-wheel or the paddles of steamboats, etc.—'''3.''' Water held or forced back, as in a mill-race or in a tributary stream, in consequence of some obstruction, as a dam or flood.—'''4.''' An artificial accumulation of water obtained at high tide and reserved in reservoirs, to be discharged at low tide for clearing off deposits in channel-beds and tideways.—'''5.''' A creek or arm of the sea which runs parallel to the coast, having only a narrow slip of land between it and the sea, and communicating with the latter by barred entrances. {{smaller block|Entering the mouth of the Moredab, an extensive ''back-water'' into which fall the Piri-Bazaar and other streams, we come alongside a fairly constructed quay. {{right|''O’Donovan'', Merv, viii.}}}} '''backwood''' (bak′wu̇d), ''n.'' That portion of a carpenter’s plane which is immediately behind the plane-iron.—'''To drive the backwood up''', {{smaller|to drive the wedge of a plane too tightly. When this is done the pressure of the plane-iron raises a bur or slight ridge at the angle of the mouth and sole.}} '''backwoods''' (bak′wu̇dz′), ''n. pl.'' Wooded or partially uncleared and unsettled districts in the remote parts of a new country; hence, in the United States and Canada, any rough or thinly settled region far from the centers of population. {{smaller block|The very ease with which books containing the world’s best literature were obtainable in the ''backwoods'' made our early writers copyists. {{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|He [Count Tolstoi] put into my hands a letter from some man living in a village in the ''backwoods'' of Pennsylvania. {{right|''The Century'', XXXIV. 261.}}}} '''backwoodsman''' (bak′wu̇dz′man), ''n.''; pl. ''backwoodsmen'' (-men). An inhabitant of the backwoods. {{smaller block|The General Boone, ''backwoodsman'' of Kentucky, Was happiest among mortals anywhere. {{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, viii. 61.}}}} '''backworm''' (bak′wėrm), ''n.'' A small worm generally found in the thin skin about the reins of hawks. See ''filander''1. '''backwort''' (bak′wėrt), ''n.'' The comfrey, ''Symphytum officinale.'' '''back-wounding''' (bak′wön″ding), ''a.'' Wounding at the back or behind one’s back; backbiting; injuring surreptitiously: as, “''backwounding'' calumny,” ''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2. '''bacon''' (bā′kon or -kn), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bakon'', ''baken'', < ME. ''bacon'', ''bacoun'', ''bakoun'', < OF. ''bacon'' = Pr. ''bacon'', < ML. ''baco(n-)'', bacon, side of bacon, shoulder, ham, also a swine, < OHG. ''bahho'', ''bacho'', MHG. ''bache'', side of bacon, ham, G. ''bache'', a wild sow (obs. or dial., a ham), = MD. ''bake'', bacon, ham, a swine, < OHG. *''bah'', etc., = AS. ''bæc'', E. ''back''1: see ''back''1.]   '''1.''' Hog’s flesh, especially the back and sides, salted or pickled and dried, usually in smoke.—'''2†.''' Pork.—'''3†.''' A hog; hence, a grossly fat person.—'''4†.''' A rustic; a clown: in allusion to the fact that swine’s flesh was the meat chiefly eaten by the rural population.   ''N. E. D.'' {{smaller block|On, ''bacons'', on! {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 2.}}}} '''To save one’s bacon,''' {{smaller|to preserve one’s self from harm.}} {{smaller block|But here I say the Turks were much mistaken, Who, hating hogs, yet wished ''to save their bacon.'' {{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, vii. 42.}}}} '''bacon-beetle''' (bā′kọn-bē″tl), ''n.'' A species of the genus ''Dermestes'', ''D. lardarius'', family ''Dermestidæ'', order ''Coleoptera'', whose larvæ are very destructive to stuffed animals in museums. The larvæ are hairy, and whitish-brown in color. {{img float|file=century v01 p0441 c3f1.png|width=193px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Bacon-Beetle (''Dermestes lardarius'').
''a'', larva; ''b'', one of its barbed hairs; ''c'', beetle. (Hair-lines show natural sizes.)}}}} '''Baconian''' (bạ̄-kō′ni-an), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< Francis ''Bacon'', born 1561, died 1626.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam, commonly called Lord Bacon: as, the ''Baconian'' philosophy.—'''Baconian method''', {{smaller|a term often, though incorrectly, applied to the method of}}
